lines.text: From space, at night, Egypt is almost completely dark.
Except for one line.
More than 100 million people, packed along a single river.
This is how that line was drawn, and why it is now under pressure.
Egypt is bigger than France and Germany put together.
But about 95% of Egyptians live along the Nile, on roughly 4% of the land.
The rest is the Sahara. Cairo gets less than 3 cm of rain in a whole year.
So about 97% of Egypt's water comes from one river.
And along most of its length, the green strip it waters is narrow.
Near Qena, we measured it on a 2025 satellite image.
At the narrowest point, the whole strip is just 8.4 km wide.
Fields, villages, roads, and the river itself. Sand on both sides.
For thousands of years, that strip was made by a flood.
Every summer, rain in the Ethiopian highlands swelled the Nile, and the river spilled over its banks.
When the water drew back, it left a layer of dark, fertile mud.
Ancient Egyptians called their country Kemet. The black land.
Then, in 1970, Egypt finished the Aswan High Dam.
Behind it grew Lake Nasser, one of the largest man-made lakes in the world.
It stretches about 550 km, from Egypt into Sudan.
The dam ended the floods. It gave Egypt water all year round, and electricity.
But it also stopped the mud. More than 98% of the river's sediment now settles in the lake.
Farmers downstream had to replace the river's mud with fertiliser. And the coast lost its supply of new land.
This is Rosetta, where one branch of the Nile meets the Mediterranean.
In 1972, the river mouth reached far out to sea, built up over centuries of Nile mud.
Here is the same place in 2025.
The tip of the land has pulled back 3.8 km. We measured it on the two images.
Without new mud, the sea kept eating the coast, until Egypt built a sea wall here in the early '90s.
Today, this coast is held in place by concrete, not by the river.
And much of the northern delta lies barely above sea level.

title: A city on its own fields

lines.text: Meanwhile, the people kept coming.
Egypt had about 27 million people in 1960. Today it has more than 109 million.
Cairo alone has roughly 25 million. It is the largest city in Africa.
This is Cairo in 1984.
And this is Cairo in 2025.
New cities have spread into the sand on both sides. But Cairo has also grown over its own fields.
Comparing the two images, roughly 1 in 4 of the fields that were green here in 1984 are now built over.
Most of it happened one building at a time, as villages and towns spread into the fields around them.
In a country with so little farmland, every field lost to concrete is hard to replace.
So Egypt is trying to move people out of the valley.
East of Cairo, this was empty sand in 2015.
Ten years later, it is a new capital city, with government ministries and the tallest building in Africa.
Whether millions of people will follow is still an open question.
Far to the south, the river is pushed into the desert too.
In wet years, Lake Nasser overflows into the Toshka depression, and lakes appear where there was only sand.
They first formed in 1998, and they grow and shrink with the floods.
Next to them, new farms are now watered from the lake. Green circles, in one of the driest places on Earth.
From space, Egypt is still one bright line.
A line drawn by a river, held in place by a dam, and squeezed by more than a hundred million people.
Which country should we look at next? Tell us in the comments.
